meta.description: Four common approaches, eight criteria, and what Planner does not have yet. No product is targeted.

accueil.texte: Four common ways to run a school, and what Planner adds.

entete.titre: Planner and the other ways of working.
entete.accroche: Four common approaches, eight criteria, and what Planner does not have yet. No product is targeted.

methode.texte: Prepared on {date}. Each Planner cell describes what the application does on that date. The other columns describe common practices, without targeting any product. What Planner lacks is marked “Coming soon”.

calcul.critere: A timetable calculated from your rules

cases.texte: Planner places sessions while keeping rooms, teachers, groups, availability and travel between campuses together. Strict rules are always kept, flexible rules as far as possible.
The grid is built by hand, often by a single person. The spreadsheet is flexible and everyone knows it.
The timetable is one module among others: depending on the tool, it is entered by hand or generated. In return, the ERP covers the whole management of the school.
The platform organises courses online. The timetable comes from another tool.
These tools focus on students, absences, grades and families. The timetable is usually entered by hand.
When a session cannot be placed, Planner names the rule that blocks it. You fix the data or relax the rule, then run the calculation again.
The spreadsheet does not flag conflicts: you find them by reading through the grid.
Depending on the tool, a room or teacher booked twice is flagged when it is entered.
Without a timetable, the question does not arise.
When the tool keeps the timetable, it usually checks conflicts as they are entered.

report.critere: A session change, tracked from end to end

cases.texte: The teacher asks, the registrar approves, the students concerned are notified, and the timetable is up to date for everyone.
The change goes out in a messaging group, and the grid is corrected separately. It is quick: everyone already has messaging on their phone.
The session is changed in the module. How students are told depends on the tool and its settings.
A course announcement tells those enrolled. The timetable is kept elsewhere.
These tools can notify families, through an app or notifications. The request and approval process depends on the tool.
A projected QR code that changes every 30 seconds. Or attendance by hand: present, late, absent.
A register or attendance sheet, then copied into a spreadsheet or the state platform. Paper works everywhere.
Attendance sheets and their statistics are usually part of the ERP.
Online presence is tracked through logins. Attendance in the classroom depends on the tool.
Absences are at the heart of these tools, often with a message to families.

Scanning goes through the Planner app. An account is linked to one phone, and one phone checks in only one student per session. The code changes every 30 seconds. If the teacher wishes, a surprise check calls out a few students marked present, at random.
Attendance relies on the teacher, who sees who is in the room.
Depending on the tool, advanced attendance, sometimes biometric, is available, often in a higher edition.
A login shows that an account was opened, not that a student is in the room.
The teacher or school office records the absence: attendance relies on their record.

compte.critere: Attendance, quizzes and games, with one account

cases.texte: Attendance, quizzes, games and the course space open with the same account.
Each task has its own tool and account. Each one is simple, and many are free.
Management and courses share the account when the ERP has its own course module. Revision games are rare there.
Courses, quizzes and resources share an account. The timetable and classroom attendance are elsewhere.
Absences, grades and families share an account. Courses and quizzes often go through another platform.

sansTelephone.critere: Without the student's phone, with what the school has

cases.texte: Attendance is taken by hand. The Linux terminal is played on the board: the teacher types the command the class suggests. The timetable prints as a PDF or opens in a browser. Quizzes and simulations need one device per student: a phone or a school computer.
Paper and the board ask nothing of students. Messaging, however, assumes a phone for the student or their parents.
Staff work on a computer. Students and families go through a portal or an app.
The platform assumes each student has a device and a connection.
Staff enter data on a computer. Families follow through an app or a portal.

sansReseau.critere: Weeks already viewed, readable without a network

cases.texte: In the app, today's board and the weeks already viewed stay readable without a network, with the time of their last update. They are erased when you sign out. An app fully usable offline is in preparation.
A printed grid can be read anywhere, without a network. It does not follow changes made after printing.
Depending on the tool, a mobile app keeps some data without a network. Office work needs a connection.
Some platforms let students download courses to follow them without a network. The timetable is not there.
A few vendors announce data entry without a network.
Grades and report cards, fees and payments, and the family space are in preparation.
Files and paper receipts. It works, but the same data is entered several times.
This is its strength: admissions, fees, staff and grades in one tool.
Grades for assignments and quizzes, not fees or families.
This is its core: absences, report cards, fees and a family app.
